title: How teachers fail
hookLine: some teachers have abused trust; the tradition's own rules exist to guard against it

cards: Here's a strange instruction from the Buddha's own mouth, as the Pali Canon tells it. He tells his monks to investigate him.

Not to take his word that he's awakened, but to watch what he does over time: is his conduct clean, is anything hidden, has fame changed him? The teacher hands the students the tools to check the teacher.
Today is about why that matters, because teachers can fail.

teach.b: Start with the hard fact. In our own time, some Buddhist teachers, in Asia and in the West, monks and laypeople, have abused the trust of their students: sexually, financially, or by controlling their lives.

Their communities and students have said so publicly, and some organizations have changed their rules because of it. That's painful to hear on a path about kindness. But the tradition saw this danger early.

teach.h: THE VINAYA: RULES BUILT FROM HARM.
teach.b: In the monastic code, the Vinaya, rules come with stories: a monk did something that caused harm, and the Buddha said, from now on, not this.
Monks and nuns gather regularly to recite those rules aloud, and to confess where they've broken them. The guardrails were built in.

Then there's the teaching to the Kalamas, people confused by teachers who each praised their own way. The Buddha tells them not to go by tradition, or by a teacher's reputation, or because this one is our teacher.

When you know for yourselves that something leads to harm and suffering, he says, let it go. And there's the instruction from the hook, in the sutta about the inquirer: check even the Buddha by his conduct.
In Tibetan Buddhism, where devotion to a teacher runs deep, the tradition also advises that a student examine a teacher carefully, for a long time, before taking them on.
So here are warning signs the tradition itself would recognize: a teacher who can't be questioned; secrecy; demands for money, sex or total obedience; being told to cut off the people who love you.
Trust is part of practice. Checking is part of it too.

how: Monastic communities recite the Vinaya rules together and confess offenses, and some Buddhist organizations now publish ethics guidelines and grievance procedures for teachers, encouraging students to raise concerns openly.

a monk who has broken the rules
the inquirer, who checks a teacher

games.q: the Kalamas are confused: teacher after teacher praises his own way. what does the Buddha tell them?
o: know for yourselves what leads to harm, and let it go
games.why: he tells them not to go by tradition or reputation, or because this one is our teacher, but by what they know leads to harm or to good.

practice: Let the warning signs come back slowly, and choose the one that stands out to you; hold it calmly, the way you'd remember where the fire exit is.

This isn't suspicion of anyone in particular; it's knowing the exit, so you can rest in the room. If any of this touches something in your own life, it's wise to talk to someone you trust outside the group.

wordCard.voice: Vimamsaka. The inquirer, the title of the sutta where the Buddha tells monks to investigate even him, a guard against abuse of trust.

orig.note: Pali vimamsaka: the inquirer, the title of the sutta where the Buddha invites monks to examine him.

carryVoice: Your line: trust, but check. Even the Buddha asked to be checked. Until tomorrow.
